overview: This resolution marks the 15th anniversary of the January 8, 2011, shooting in Tucson, Arizona, at a public event hosted by then-Congresswoman Gabby Giffords, in which 6 people were killed and 13, including Giffords, were wounded. It honors those killed, including a federal judge, a congressional staff member and a 9-year-old girl, and supports the survivors and their families. It recognizes Giffords' work since the attack to promote civility and prevent gun violence, commends the people of Tucson and first responders, and reaffirms Congress's commitment to respectful dialogue and condemning political violence. It is a concurrent resolution, meaning both chambers must agree to it, and it has no force of law. The Senate passed it on February 5, 2026, and as of February 13, 2026, it was awaiting action in the House.
for: Supporters say honoring the victims and survivors of the Tucson attack is a fitting way to condemn political violence and reaffirm basic civility in public life.
against: Critics say the resolution is symbolic and does not change any law, and some may object to its praise of Giffords' gun violence prevention advocacy as taking a side on gun policy.
